```{r setup, include = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
# the code of the benchmark is in the script code/clumppling_benchmark.R,
# from which the chunks below are read (purl = FALSE because pkgdown purls
# this file from the package root when looking for images, where this
# relative path does not exist)
knitr::read_chunk("code/clumppling_benchmark.R")
# the directory with the results of the benchmark
results_dir <- params$results_dir
```

`gt_clumppling()` aligns the clusters of replicate runs of ADMIXTURE-like
analyses, and groups the runs into modes, with the method of clumppling
(Liu, Kopelman & Rosenberg 2024). Its R and C++ code is ported, with
modifications, from the python package clumppling (version 2.0.10, by Xiran
Liu), which previous versions of `tidygenclust` ran through `reticulate`. This article compares the two
implementations: do they give the same results, and how long do they take?

The comparison uses the two example datasets of the python clumppling,
which are also analysed in the paper that describes it (Liu, Kopelman &
Rosenberg 2024), and which `tidygenclust` includes as `gt_admix` objects
(in `inst/extdata`):

- capeverde: 200 runs of ADMIXTURE (50 for each K from 2 to 5) on the Cape
  Verde data of Verdu et al. (2017), with 399 individuals (44 Cape
  Verdeans, and 355 individuals from British, French, Iberian, Gambian and
  Mandenka populations);
- chicken: 60 runs of STRUCTURE (20 for each of K = 17, 19 and 21) on the
  chicken data of Rosenberg et al. (2001), with 600 chickens from 20
  breeds.

```{r results-read, include = FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
# the time of each run, and the agreement of the results of the two
# implementations on each dataset
timings <- read.csv(file.path(results_dir, "timings.csv"))
agreement <- read.csv(file.path(results_dir, "agreement.csv"))
startup <- read.csv(file.path(results_dir, "startup.csv"))
session <- read.csv(file.path(results_dir, "session.csv"))
implementation_labels <- c(r = "gt_clumppling()", python = "python clumppling")
setting_labels <- c(
  memory = "In memory",
  files = "From Q files",
  command_line = "From the command line"
)
# the median time of each implementation on each dataset, in each setting
times <- timings %>%
  group_by(dataset, setting, implementation) %>%
  summarise(seconds = median(seconds), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = implementation, values_from = seconds) %>%
  left_join(agreement, by = "dataset") %>%
  mutate(speed_up = python / r) %>%
  arrange(
    factor(setting, names(setting_labels)),
    desc(n_individuals == 399),
    n_runs
  )
n_repeats <- n_distinct(timings$repeat_run)
format_seconds <- function(x) {
  formatC(signif(x, 2), format = "fg", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
}
format_diff <- function(x) {
  ifelse(is.na(x), "-", formatC(signif(x, 2), format = "g", digits = 2))
}
time_of <- function(dataset, implementation, setting = "memory") {
  times[[implementation]][times$dataset == dataset & times$setting == setting]
}
speed_up_of <- function(dataset, setting = "memory") {
  round(time_of(dataset, "python", setting) / time_of(dataset, "r", setting))
}
startup_of <- function(implementation) {
  median(startup$seconds[startup$implementation == implementation])
}
```

# Results

## Summary

- With the Q matrices already in memory, on the 200 runs of the capeverde
  data (399 individuals, K = 2 to 5), `gt_clumppling()` took
  `r format_seconds(time_of("capeverde_50", "r"))` s and the python
  implementation `r format_seconds(time_of("capeverde_50", "python"))` s,
  about `r speed_up_of("capeverde_50")` times longer. On the 60 runs of the
  chicken data (600 individuals, K = 17, 19 and 21), they took
  `r format_seconds(time_of("chicken_20", "r"))` s and
  `r format_seconds(time_of("chicken_20", "python"))` s.
- Starting from Q files adds the time taken to read them: on the 200
  capeverde runs, `r format_seconds(time_of("capeverde_50", "r", "files"))`
  s and `r format_seconds(time_of("capeverde_50", "python", "files"))` s.
  In R, reading the files takes longer than `gt_clumppling()` itself.
- From the command line, each implementation also has to start, and load
  its packages: about `r format_seconds(startup_of("r"))` s for R and
  `r format_seconds(startup_of("python"))` s for python. With few runs, this
  is most of the time, and the difference shrinks: with 5 runs for each K,
  `r format_seconds(time_of("capeverde_5", "r", "command_line"))` s and
  `r format_seconds(time_of("capeverde_5", "python", "command_line"))` s.
  With 200 runs, it is still
  `r format_seconds(time_of("capeverde_50", "r", "command_line"))` s
  against
  `r format_seconds(time_of("capeverde_50", "python", "command_line"))` s.
- The two implementations found the same modes in
  `r sum(agreement$same_modes)` of the `r nrow(agreement)` datasets. Where
  the modes were the same, their aligned ancestry proportions differed by
  at most `r format_diff(max(agreement$max_diff_aligned, na.rm = TRUE))`.
  On the chicken data, the modes were the same for K =
  `r agreement$same_modes_k[agreement$dataset == "chicken_20"]` only, as
  expected (see below).

## Do they give the same results?

Both implementations were run with the default options (`use_rep = TRUE`,
`merge = TRUE`, `cd_method = "louvain"`, `use_best_pair = TRUE`) and the
same seed. Each implementation runs the same code whether the Q matrices
are in memory, read from Q files or the analysis is run from the command
line (see below), so the results were compared once, with the Q matrices
in memory:

```{r table-agreement, echo = FALSE}
agreement %>%
  mutate(
    same_modes_k = if_else(same_modes_k == "", "none", same_modes_k),
    same_representatives = if_else(same_representatives, "yes", "no"),
    across(c(max_diff_aligned, max_diff_cost), format_diff)
  ) %>%
  select(
    dataset, n_runs, n_individuals, k_values, n_modes_r, n_modes_python,
    same_modes_k, same_representatives, max_diff_aligned, max_diff_cost
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Dataset", "Runs", "Individuals", "K", "Modes (R)", "Modes (python)",
      "K with the same modes", "Same representatives",
      "Largest difference (modes)",
      "Largest difference (costs)"
    ),
    align = "lrrlrrllrr",
    caption = paste0(
      "Number of modes found by each implementation, the values of K for ",
      "which the modes (the runs in each mode) are the same, whether the ",
      "representative runs of the modes are the same, and, where all the ",
      "modes are the same, the largest absolute differences ",
      "between the aligned ancestry proportions of the modes, and between ",
      "the costs of the alignments across K."
    )
  )
```

Where the modes are the same, the remaining differences are rounding
errors. Grouping runs into modes uses community detection (the Louvain
method, by default), which draws random numbers. `gt_clumppling()` draws
them from R's generator, so the same seed does not give the same random
choices as in python. This does not change the modes when the community
structure of the runs is clear, as in the capeverde data. It can when the
structure is ambiguous, as for K = 17 and 19 in the chicken data, where the
modes found by python itself change with the seed. The test suite of
`tidygenclust` checks that, given the same modes, the two implementations
give the same results on these data.

## How long do they take?

The two implementations are typically used in different ways. In R, the Q
matrices are usually already in memory, in a `gt_admix` object returned by
`gt_admixture()` or by `tidypopgen::read_q_files()`, and `gt_clumppling()`
returns its results as an R object. The python clumppling is usually run
as a command-line tool, which starts python, loads its packages, reads the
Q files, and writes its results to files. Timing `gt_clumppling()` on a
`gt_admix` object against the command-line tool would flatter
`gt_clumppling()`. So we timed each implementation in three settings:

- **In memory**: the Q matrices are already in memory, and R or python is
  already running, with the packages loaded. This times the method alone.
  In python, the Q matrices are converted to numpy arrays before the timing
  starts, and the results are left as python objects, so the time taken to
  pass data between R and python (with `reticulate`) is not included.
- **From Q files**: as above, but starting from a directory of Q files, one
  for each run. In R, they are read with `tidypopgen::read_q_files()`. In
  python, they are read by clumppling's own parser, which writes the
  processed matrices to a directory and reads them back, as the
  command-line tool does.
- **From the command line**: each run is a new process, which starts R or
  python, loads the packages, reads the Q files, and saves the results. In
  R, this is a script run with `Rscript`, which loads `tidygenclust` and
  saves the results with `saveRDS()`. In python, it is the command-line
  tool of clumppling, without figures (`-v False`).

The last setting is the closest to the time a user waits, but the two
implementations still do slightly different things: the command-line tool
of clumppling writes more output than `saveRDS()` (the processed Q files,
the alignment of every pair of runs, the modes and their statistics, and a
log).

```{r plot-timings, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.8}
implementation_colours <- c(r = "#2a78d6", python = "#eb6834")
# the number of runs of each dataset (capeverde, unless stated)
dataset_labels <- if_else(
  agreement$n_individuals == 399,
  as.character(agreement$n_runs),
  paste0(agreement$n_runs, "\n(chicken)")
)
timings %>%
  left_join(agreement, by = "dataset") %>%
  mutate(
    dataset = factor(dataset, agreement$dataset, dataset_labels),
    setting = factor(setting, names(setting_labels), setting_labels),
    implementation = factor(implementation, names(implementation_labels))
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = dataset, y = seconds, colour = implementation)) +
  stat_summary(
    data = function(d) filter(d, n_individuals == 399),
    aes(group = implementation),
    fun = median,
    geom = "line",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~setting) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = implementation_colours,
    labels = implementation_labels
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of runs (capeverde data, and chicken data)",
    y = "Time (s, log scale)",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "top")
```

```{r table-timings, echo = FALSE}
times %>%
  mutate(
    setting = setting_labels[setting],
    setting = if_else(duplicated(setting), "", setting),
    r = format_seconds(r),
    python = format_seconds(python),
    speed_up = formatC(speed_up, format = "f", digits = 0)
  ) %>%
  select(setting, dataset, n_runs, k_values, r, python, speed_up) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Setting", "Dataset", "Runs", "K", "gt_clumppling() (s)",
      "python (s)", "Speed-up"
    ),
    align = "llrlrrr",
    caption = paste0(
      "Median time (s) of ", n_repeats, " runs of each implementation, in ",
      "each setting, and ratio of the times of python and gt_clumppling()."
    )
  )
```

With many runs, most of the time goes into aligning every pair of runs
with the same K, so the time grows roughly with the square of the number of
runs for each K. For each pair, clumppling solves an integer linear
program with GLPK (through cvxpy), whereas `gt_clumppling()` solves the
same problem exactly as a linear assignment problem, with the Hungarian
algorithm in C++.

Reading the 200 capeverde Q files took about
`r format_seconds(time_of("capeverde_50", "r", "files") - time_of("capeverde_50", "r"))`
s in R (`tidypopgen::read_q_files()` reads each file with `read.table()`),
more than `gt_clumppling()` itself, but little compared with the time of
the python implementation, whose own parser took about
`r format_seconds(time_of("capeverde_50", "python", "files") - time_of("capeverde_50", "python"))`
s.

From the command line, starting R and loading `tidygenclust` took about
`r format_seconds(startup_of("r"))` s, and starting python and loading
clumppling (with numpy, cvxpy, cdlib and matplotlib) about
`r format_seconds(startup_of("python"))` s (medians of `r n_repeats`
runs, without doing anything else). This sets a floor to the times of both
implementations, which dominates with few runs. The rest of the time from
the command line is within about a second of the time from Q files, so
writing the results takes little time, although clumppling writes more of
them.

# How the benchmark was run

The benchmark is run with the script
`vignettes/articles/code/clumppling_benchmark.R` (in the source code of the
package), which saves its results in
`vignettes/articles/data/clumppling_benchmark`; this article reads them
from there. The code below is taken from that script.

The python implementation is run with the wrapper that previous versions of
`tidygenclust` used, which is now used to create the reference results of
the tests (`data-raw/clumppling/py_clumppling.R`). It runs in the conda
environment created by `data-raw/clumppling/setup_clumppling_env.sh`, with
clumppling 2.0.10 and pinned versions of its dependencies:

```{r clump-setup, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r clump-python, eval = FALSE}
```

The datasets are the example datasets of clumppling (see the
introduction), and subsets of the capeverde data with fewer runs for each
K.
Each is also written as a directory of Q files, and converted to numpy
arrays:

```{r clump-data, eval = FALSE}
```

The results of the two implementations are compared with:

```{r clump-compare, eval = FALSE}
```

The runs that are timed, in each setting, are:

```{r clump-settings, eval = FALSE}
```

Each implementation is run on each dataset once in memory, to compare the
results, and once from the Q files, and then timed `r n_repeats` times in
each setting:

```{r clump-runs, eval = FALSE}
```

Finally, the time taken to start R or python and load the packages is
timed on its own:

```{r clump-startup, eval = FALSE}
```

## Running the benchmark again

Install `tidygenclust` with `R CMD INSTALL`, rather than loading it with
`devtools::load_all()`, which compiles its C++ code without optimisation.
Create the conda environment with the python implementation (from the root
of the package):

```sh
bash data-raw/clumppling/setup_clumppling_env.sh
```

or set `CLUMPPLING_REFERENCE_ENV` to the name of another conda environment
with the same versions of the python packages. Then run, from
`vignettes/articles`, on an otherwise idle machine:

```sh
cd vignettes/articles
Rscript code/clumppling_benchmark.R
```

This takes a few minutes. Then render this article again.
